opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest answer is that the line between the two is blurrier than people assume, and it's getting blurrier over time.

The way I think about it, an environment is really just three things: a set of tasks, a harness that lets the model interact with the world, and some way of scoring what happened. If you already have an agent application in production, you have two of those three pieces. You have the harness, the tools, the scaffolding, the system prompts, all the context management. And you have real tasks coming in from users. What you're often missing is the reward signal, some reliable way of saying "this trajectory was good, this one was bad."

So my default bias is that if you're building a product and you want the model to get better at that product, you should try to make the application itself the environment as much as possible. The closer your training setup matches the conditions the model will actually see at inference time, the less you have to worry about distribution shift. If you train in some clean, toy version of your codebase or your tool set and then deploy into the messy real thing, you'll often find the gains don't transfer the way you hoped. The model learns quirks of the sandbox rather than the skill you care about.

Where dedicated environments make sense is when you need things the production app can't give you. One is control. In production you can't reset the world, you can't run the same task a thousand times with different rollouts, and you often can't safely let the model take destructive actions. Another is verifiability. A lot of the most effective RL right now comes from tasks where you can check the answer cheaply and robustly, like unit tests, math answers, or structured outputs. Real user interactions often don't have that, so you end up building something more synthetic to get a crisp signal. And the third is targeting specific capabilities. If you know your model is weak at, say, long-horizon planning or recovering from tool errors, it can be more efficient to build focused environments that hammer on that skill than to wait for it to show up naturally in your traffic.

In practice I think the best approach is kind of a hybrid. You start from your actual application, you wrap it so it can be run in a reproducible, sandboxed way, and then you invest heavily in the rubric or verifier layer. That's where a lot of the real work is. Writing good reward functions, figuring out which parts can be checked programmatically and which need an LLM judge, and making sure the model can't just game the scoring.

The other thing I'd say is that the tooling has gotten a lot better here. A couple of years ago, setting up RL was this specialized research-lab activity, and environments were bespoke one-off things. Now it's much more feasible for an application team to say, "here's our agent, here's how we score it, let's run training against it." That's a big part of why I'm excited about treating environments as something more like software artifacts that people can share, compose, and iterate on, rather than something that only lives inside a big lab.

So the short version is: lean toward your real application as the environment, because that's where the signal you actually care about lives, and build dedicated environments when you need control, clean verification, or targeted pressure on a specific weakness.

r002.rationale: It recommends using the production application itself as the environment and notes that real user tasks and the production setup help align training with inference.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that for most people the application already is the environment, and the question is really whether you're willing to admit that. When you build an agent product, you've already made all the hard decisions that define an RL environment. You've picked the tools, you've picked the observation format, you've picked what the model sees after each action. The thing you're usually missing is a reward signal and a way to reset state cheaply. So when people say "should we build a dedicated environment," what they're often actually asking is "should we go build a toy version of our product that's easier to run a thousand times in parallel." And sometimes the answer is yes, but you have to be clear-eyed that you're paying a tax in fidelity to buy that convenience.

The case for a dedicated environment is mostly about iteration speed and control. If your real system hits a live database, calls third-party APIs, has rate limits, has side effects you can't undo, you can't just spin up ten thousand episodes and let the model flail. You need something sandboxed, resettable, and ideally deterministic enough that when a run goes badly you can figure out whether it was the policy or the environment that was flaky. Dedicated environments also let you shape the curriculum. You can make easy versions, you can inject specific failure modes, you can build verifiers that are much cleaner than anything you'd get from real usage. That's really valuable early on, when the model just can't do the task yet and you need a dense enough signal to get off the ground.

The case for training directly against the application is that the distribution is real. Every simplification you make in a dedicated environment is a place where the model can learn something that doesn't transfer. The tool outputs are slightly cleaner, the errors are less weird, the tasks are more well-posed than what users actually ask. And the model will absolutely exploit that. It'll learn to be good at your environment rather than good at the job. So the pattern I like is to think of the dedicated environment as a staging area, not the destination. You use it to bootstrap, to get the model from "can't do it" to "does it sometimes," and then you want the loop to close against something as close to production as you can tolerate.

Practically, the thing that unlocks that is investing in the harness rather than in a parallel world. If you build your application so the agent loop is already a clean interface where you can swap the backend, snapshot state, replay trajectories, and attach a scorer, then you get the dedicated environment almost for free as a mode of the real thing rather than a fork of it. The failure mode I see most is teams that build a beautiful RL gym for six months, get great numbers on it, and then discover the gap to the actual product is bigger than the gap they started with. So my bias is: build the environment inside the application, make the sandbox a flag rather than a separate repo, and only carve out a truly separate environment when there's a concrete reason, like safety, cost, or a skill that you genuinely need to drill in isolation before it's useful in context.

r002.rationale: It says the agent product application is usually already the environment and recommends training against the application itself, which communicates using the product interface as the RL environment.

r003.rationale: It recommends building a harness with backend swapping, state snapshots, trajectory replay, and scoring, but does not say infrastructure used to evaluate agent system configurations can also support RL.

astra-6.text:
I think the default should be to make the application itself the environment, if you can. The agent is going to operate with a particular set of tools, information, and constraints, so having it learn in that same setting reduces the gap between what you train and what you actually want it to do.

But an application isn’t automatically a useful training environment. You need a way to give it tasks, evaluate the outcomes, and reset things so you can run lots of attempts. And you need to do that without, you know, sending real emails or breaking somebody’s database. Building that infrastructure can be a substantial part of the work.

Dedicated environments make sense when there’s a specific capability you want to isolate, or when the real application is too slow, expensive, or difficult to evaluate. You can make the feedback much cleaner. The risk is that you end up training something that’s very good at your simplified task, and the improvement doesn’t carry over.

So I’d start with the actual behavior you want in the application and work backward. What can you evaluate reliably? What can you run repeatedly? Then build a dedicated environment where it helps you get more useful practice, and keep checking that the gains show up in the application.

r002.rationale: It recommends making the application itself the environment by default, but does not specify the criterion’s case: a product interface through which end users interact with an agent.

r003.rationale: It says an environment needs task, evaluation, and reset infrastructure, but does not state that infrastructure already used to evaluate agent system configurations can also support reinforcement learning.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the default should be to make the application itself the environment, whenever you can. If you already have an agent doing a task, with tools and some way to tell whether it succeeded, that’s most of what you need. You can run it, collect trajectories, and train against the thing you actually want it to get better at.

The reason to build a dedicated environment is usually that something about that loop is missing. Maybe the real task takes a week, or it’s expensive to run, or you can’t safely let the model explore. Maybe you need to reset the world to a particular state and try again. Then a separate environment can make the feedback loop much faster and more controllable.

But you have to be careful about the gap you introduce. It’s very easy to build something where reward goes up and the agent gets better at your environment, but that improvement doesn’t carry over to the application. So I’d start with the actual task and ask: what’s preventing us from training here? Then build the infrastructure or simulation needed to remove that bottleneck.
